claim: The three cohorts enrolled a total of 1021 children aged 6 months to 10 years from 331 randomly chosen households across the three study sites.
source: The three cohorts enrolled a total of 1021 children aged 6 months to 10 years from 331 randomly chosen households across the three study sites.
evidence: This is directly stated in the manuscript text and represents a factual description of the study population.

claim: The analysis was limited to data from 773 children who experienced at least one patent P. falciparum infection between August 2011 and November 2014.
source: This analysis was limited to data from 773 children who experienced at least one patent P. falciparum infection between August 2011 and November 2014.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the manuscript as a description of the analytical sample.

claim: Participants living in Nagongera experienced the highest incidences of symptomatic malaria with a median of 2.6 episodes per person year.
source: Participants living in Nagongera experienced the highest incidences of symptomatic malaria (median 2.6 episodes per person year), followed by those living in Kihihi (median 1.6 episodes per person year) and Walukuba (median 0.6 episodes per person year) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1 showing measured incidence rates.

claim: Participants living in Kihihi experienced a median of 1.6 episodes of symptomatic malaria per person year.
source: Participants living in Nagongera experienced the highest incidences of symptomatic malaria (median 2.6 episodes per person year), followed by those living in Kihihi (median 1.6 episodes per person year) and Walukuba (median 0.6 episodes per person year) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Participants living in Walukuba experienced a median of 0.6 episodes of symptomatic malaria per person year.
source: Participants living in Nagongera experienced the highest incidences of symptomatic malaria (median 2.6 episodes per person year), followed by those living in Kihihi (median 1.6 episodes per person year) and Walukuba (median 0.6 episodes per person year) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Nagongera had significantly higher annual entomological inoculation rates with a median of 51 infectious bites per year (range 10–582).
source: These incidences were consistent with results from monthly entomological surveys conducted in all cohort households, with significantly higher annual entomological inoculation rates (aEIR) recorded in Nagongera (median 51 infectious bites per year, range 10–582) as compared to Kihihi (median 8 infectious bites per year, range 4–47) and Walukuba (median 2 infectious bites per year, range 1–8).
evidence: This is supported by entomological survey data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Kihihi had a median annual entomological inoculation rate of 8 infectious bites per year (range 4–47).
source: These incidences were consistent with results from monthly entomological surveys conducted in all cohort households, with significantly higher annual entomological inoculation rates (aEIR) recorded in Nagongera (median 51 infectious bites per year, range 10–582) as compared to Kihihi (median 8 infectious bites per year, range 4–47) and Walukuba (median 2 infectious bites per year, range 1–8).
evidence: This is supported by entomological survey data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Walukuba had a median annual entomological inoculation rate of 2 infectious bites per year (range 1–8).
source: These incidences were consistent with results from monthly entomological surveys conducted in all cohort households, with significantly higher annual entomological inoculation rates (aEIR) recorded in Nagongera (median 51 infectious bites per year, range 10–582) as compared to Kihihi (median 8 infectious bites per year, range 4–47) and Walukuba (median 2 infectious bites per year, range 1–8).
evidence: This is supported by entomological survey data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The prevalence of asymptomatic parasitemia was highest in Nagongera.
source: Interestingly, prevalence of asymptomatic parasitemia did not follow this same relationship; the prevalence of asymptomatic parasitemia was highest in Nagongera, and prevalences in the lower transmission sites were similar.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be inferred from Table 1 data.

claim: Prevalences of asymptomatic parasitemia in the lower transmission sites (Kihihi and Walukuba) were similar.
source: Interestingly, prevalence of asymptomatic parasitemia did not follow this same relationship; the prevalence of asymptomatic parasitemia was highest in Nagongera, and prevalences in the lower transmission sites were similar.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be inferred from Table 1 data.

claim: There was a significant correlation between aEIR and individual hazard of infection across sites (R2 = 0.47, p<0.001).
source: We found a significant correlation between these two independent metrics of exposure across sites (R2 = 0.47, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In Nagongera, aEIR explained 3% of the variance in individual hazard of infection (R2 = 0.03, p=0.004).
source: aEIR explained less of the variance between individuals within each site: Nagongera (R2 = 0.03, p=0.004); Kihihi (R2 = 0.12, p<0.001); Walukuba (0.01, p=0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-site correlation analysis.

claim: In Kihihi, aEIR explained 12% of the variance in individual hazard of infection (R2 = 0.12, p<0.001).
source: aEIR explained less of the variance between individuals within each site: Nagongera (R2 = 0.03, p=0.004); Kihihi (R2 = 0.12, p<0.001); Walukuba (0.01, p=0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-site correlation analysis.

claim: In Walukuba, aEIR explained 1% of the variance in individual hazard of infection (R2 = 0.01, p=0.05).
source: aEIR explained less of the variance between individuals within each site: Nagongera (R2 = 0.03, p=0.004); Kihihi (R2 = 0.12, p<0.001); Walukuba (0.01, p=0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-site correlation analysis.

claim: Parasite densities developed upon infection decreased with increasing age in all settings for both symptomatic and asymptomatic infections.
source: Parasite densities developed upon infection decreased with increasing age in all settings and for both symptomatic (passive detection) and asymptomatic (detected during routine visits) infections.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: A trend toward lower parasite densities was observed among individuals living in settings with higher aEIRs (Nagongera) compared to settings with lower aEIR (Kihihi and Walukuba).
source: A trend toward lower parasite densities was also observed among individuals living in settings with higher aEIRs (Nagongera), as compared to settings with lower aEIR (Kihihi and Walukuba).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Models allowing smooth (non-linear) relationships with aEIR best fit the anti-parasite immunity data.
source: We considered multiple candidate models to describe the association between parasite density, age and aEIR (Appendix 1). Models allowing smooth (non-linear) relationships with aEIR best fit the data.
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: Models allowing for two-way interactions between age and aEIR outperformed models that did not include interactions.
source: Models allowing for two-way interactions between age and aEIR also outperformed models that did not include interactions.
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: In moderate and high transmission settings (households with aEIR >5), parasite densities decreased by a factor of 0.76 (95%CI 0.75–0.77) for each additional year of age.
source: In moderate and high transmission settings (households with aEIR >5), increasing age and increasing exposure were independently and linearly associated with decreases in the parasite densities (Table 2). On average, parasite densities decreased by a factor of 0.76 (95%CI 0.75–0.77) for each additional year of age and by a factor of 0.73 (95%CI 0.70–0.76) for each two-fold increase in the aEIR.
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression modeling presented in Table 2.

claim: In moderate and high transmission settings (households with aEIR >5), parasite densities decreased by a factor of 0.73 (95%CI 0.70–0.76) for each two-fold increase in the aEIR.
source: In moderate and high transmission settings (households with aEIR >5), increasing age and increasing exposure were independently and linearly associated with decreases in the parasite densities (Table 2). On average, parasite densities decreased by a factor of 0.76 (95%CI 0.75–0.77) for each additional year of age and by a factor of 0.73 (95%CI 0.70–0.76) for each two-fold increase in the aEIR.
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression modeling presented in Table 2.

claim: An individual aged 1 year exposed to an aEIR of 10 is expected to develop a parasite density of 14,610 parasites/μL (95% CI 5924–36,031 parasites/μL) upon infection.
source: While an individual aged 1 year exposed to an aEIR of 10 is expected to develop a parasite density of 14,610 parasites/μL (95% CI 5924–36,031 parasites/μL) upon infection, the expected parasite density goes down to 3237 parasites/μL (95% CI 1381–7586 parasites/μL) by age 10 years.
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the best fitting model.

claim: An individual aged 10 years exposed to an aEIR of 10 is expected to develop a parasite density of 3237 parasites/μL (95% CI 1381–7586 parasites/μL) upon infection.
source: While an individual aged 1 year exposed to an aEIR of 10 is expected to develop a parasite density of 14,610 parasites/μL (95% CI 5924–36,031 parasites/μL) upon infection, the expected parasite density goes down to 3237 parasites/μL (95% CI 1381–7586 parasites/μL) by age 10 years.
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the best fitting model.

claim: An individual aged 1 year living in a setting with aEIR of 150 is expected to develop a parasite density of 13,071 parasites/μL (95% CI 5256–32,503 parasites/μL) upon infection.
source: In contrast, the expected parasite density in an individual living in a setting with aEIR of 150 will be similar at age 1 year (13,071 parasites/μL (95% CI 5256–32,503 parasites/μL)), but significantly lower by age 10 years (999 parasites/μL (95% CI 398–2508 parasites/μL)).
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the best fitting model.

claim: An individual aged 10 years living in a setting with aEIR of 150 is expected to develop a parasite density of 999 parasites/μL (95% CI 398–2508 parasites/μL) upon infection.
source: In contrast, the expected parasite density in an individual living in a setting with aEIR of 150 will be similar at age 1 year (13,071 parasites/μL (95% CI 5256–32,503 parasites/μL)), but significantly lower by age 10 years (999 parasites/μL (95% CI 398–2508 parasites/μL)).
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the best fitting model.

claim: For any given level of cumulative exposure, each additional year of life was associated with decreases in parasite densities by a factor of 0.82 (95%CI 0.81–0.85).
source: Results from these models are consistent with a smaller, yet independent effect of age on the development of anti-parasite immunity; for any given level of cumulative exposure, each additional year of life was associated with decreases in parasite densities by a factor of 0.82 (95%CI 0.81–0.85).
evidence: This is a statistical result from models adjusting for cumulative exposure.

claim: Models including smooth effects and interactions fitted the anti-disease immunity data significantly better than simpler models.
source: Consistent with models characterizing anti-parasite immunity, models including smooth effects and interactions fitted the data significantly better than simpler models.
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis.

claim: There was a strong association between parasite densities and objective temperature.
source: As expected, we found a strong association between parasite densities and objective temperature (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increases in parasite densities above 1000 parasites/μL were associated with higher expected temperatures across ages and transmission settings.
source: Increases in parasite densities above 1000 parasites/μL were associated with higher expected temperatures across ages and transmission settings.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by modeling results.

claim: In moderate and high transmission settings (aEIR >5), the objective temperature at a given parasite density decreased on average by 0.08°C (95% CI 0.07–0.10°C) for each additional year of life.
source: In moderate and high transmission settings (aEIR >5), the objective temperature at a given parasite density decreased on average by 0.08°C (95% CI 0.07–0.10°C) for each additional year of life (Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression modeling presented in Table 2.

claim: The expected temperature for a child aged 1 year living in a setting with aEIR of 10 with a parasite density of 40,000 would be 38.8°C (95% CI 38.5–39.2°C).
source: Thus, while the expected temperature for a child aged 1 year living in a setting with aEIR of 10 with a parasite density of 40,000 would be 38.8°C (95% CI 38.5–39.2°C), the expected temperature would decrease to 37.6°C (95% CI 37.3–38.0°C) if the same child experienced the infection at age 10 years (Figures 4b and 6).
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the best fitting model.

claim: The expected temperature for a child aged 10 years living in a setting with aEIR of 10 with a parasite density of 40,000 would be 37.6°C (95% CI 37.3–38.0°C).
source: Thus, while the expected temperature for a child aged 1 year living in a setting with aEIR of 10 with a parasite density of 40,000 would be 38.8°C (95% CI 38.5–39.2°C), the expected temperature would decrease to 37.6°C (95% CI 37.3–38.0°C) if the same child experienced the infection at age 10 years (Figures 4b and 6).
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the best fitting model.

claim: For moderate and high transmission settings (aEIR 5 to 300), the objective temperature decreased by 0.07°C (95% CI 0.05–0.10°C) for each two-fold increase in aEIR.
source: For moderate and high transmission settings (aEIR 5 to 300), there was a linear negative association between objective temperature at a given parasite density and aEIR. The objective temperature decreased by 0.07°C (95% CI 0.05–0.10°C) for each two-fold increase in aEIR.
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression modeling.

claim: Children living in the lowest transmission settings (aEIR 1 to 5) appeared to tolerate higher parasite densities than children living in moderate transmission settings (aEIR 5 to 10).
source: However, the relationship did not follow this trend for lower transmission settings (Table 2). Children living in the lowest transmission settings (aEIR 1 to 5) appeared to tolerate higher parasite densities than children living in moderate transmission settings (aEIR 5 to 10).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: A 1-year-old child living in a setting with aEIR of 10 presenting with a parasite density as low as 3747 parasites/μL (95% CI 777–11,129 parasites/μL) will be expected to be febrile.
source: Thus, while a 1-year-old child living in a setting with aEIR of 10 presenting with a parasite density as low as 3747 parasites/μL (95% CI 777–11,129 parasites/μL) will be expected to be febrile, children older than 6 years of age exposed to very high transmission (aEIR 150) might be afebrile even with parasite densities higher than 60,000 parasites/μL.
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the fever threshold analysis.

claim: Children older than 6 years of age exposed to very high transmission (aEIR 150) might be afebrile even with parasite densities higher than 60,000 parasites/μL.
source: Thus, while a 1-year-old child living in a setting with aEIR of 10 presenting with a parasite density as low as 3747 parasites/μL (95% CI 777–11,129 parasites/μL) will be expected to be febrile, children older than 6 years of age exposed to very high transmission (aEIR 150) might be afebrile even with parasite densities higher than 60,000 parasites/μL.
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the fever threshold analysis.

claim: The expected probability of symptomatic disease for a child aged 1 year living in a setting with aEIR of 50 is 0.92 (95% CI 0.79–0.97).
source: The expected probability of symptomatic disease for a child aged 1 year living in a setting with aEIR of 50 is 0.92 (95% CI 0.79–0.97), but it decreases to 0.51 (95% CI 0.29–0.73) by age 10 years.
evidence: This is a model prediction from the overall immunity analysis.

claim: The expected probability of symptomatic disease for a child aged 10 years living in a setting with aEIR of 50 is 0.51 (95% CI 0.29–0.73).
source: The expected probability of symptomatic disease for a child aged 1 year living in a setting with aEIR of 50 is 0.92 (95% CI 0.79–0.97), but it decreases to 0.51 (95% CI 0.29–0.73) by age 10 years.
evidence: This is a model prediction from the overall immunity analysis.

claim: No association was found between the number of recent malaria infections and anti-parasite or anti-disease immunity outcomes.
source: We found no association between the number of recent malaria infections and our outcomes of interest (Appendix 2, figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from models adjusted for recent infection history.

claim: Models that included random effects at the individual and household levels outperformed models that assumed independence of observations.
source: Models that included random effects at the individual and household levels outperformed models that assumed independence of observations, consistent with large heterogeneity between individuals in the development of anti-parasite, anti-disease and overall immunity against symptomatic malaria.
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis.

claim: There is large heterogeneity between individuals in the development of anti-parasite, anti-disease and overall immunity against symptomatic malaria.
source: Models that included random effects at the individual and household levels outperformed models that assumed independence of observations, consistent with large heterogeneity between individuals in the development of anti-parasite, anti-disease and overall immunity against symptomatic malaria.
evidence: This is inferred from the model comparison results showing better fit with random effects.

claim: Anti-parasite and anti-disease immunity develop gradually and in parallel.
source: Our findings illustrate how anti-parasite and anti-disease immunity develop gradually and in parallel, complementing each other in reducing the probability of experiencing symptomatic disease upon infection with P. falciparum.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Anti-parasite immunity acts to restrict the parasite densities that develop upon each subsequent infection.
source: While anti-parasite immunity acts to restrict the parasite densities that develop upon each subsequent infection, anti-disease immunity increases the tolerance to high parasite densities.
evidence: This is a conceptual summary of the anti-parasite immunity findings.

claim: Anti-disease immunity increases the tolerance to high parasite densities.
source: While anti-parasite immunity acts to restrict the parasite densities that develop upon each subsequent infection, anti-disease immunity increases the tolerance to high parasite densities.
evidence: This is a conceptual summary of the anti-disease immunity findings.

claim: Older children are less likely to develop symptomatic malaria upon infection both because they tolerate parasite densities better without developing fever, and because they are less likely to develop high parasite densities.
source: Thus, older children are less likely to develop symptomatic malaria upon infection both because they tolerate parasite densities better without developing fever, and because they are less likely to develop high parasite densities.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating the anti-parasite and anti-disease immunity findings.

claim: There are independent effects of age on the acquisition of both anti-parasite and anti-disease immunity.
source: Our results indicate independent effects of age on the acquisition of both anti-parasite and anti-disease immunity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the modeling results showing age effects independent of exposure.

claim: The independent age effects on immunity may reflect maturation of the immune system as well as other physiological changes that decrease the propensity to fever.
source: These independent age effects may reflect maturation of the immune system as well as other physiological changes that decrease the propensity to fever (Struik and Riley, 2004; Baird, 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the age effects, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There are independent effects of transmission intensity on the acquisition of anti-parasite and anti-disease immunity.
source: Furthermore, our findings are consistent with independent effects of transmission intensity on the acquisition of these two types of immunity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the modeling results showing exposure effects independent of age.

claim: Immunity develops faster in moderate and high transmission settings where individuals get infected by P. falciparum more often.
source: While the results obtained for moderate and high transmission settings (aEIR >5) are consistent and expected, and suggest that immunity develops faster in settings where individuals get infected by P. falciparum more often, the results obtained for the lowest transmission settings are harder to reconcile.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the results for moderate and high transmission settings.

claim: The discrepant results for the lowest transmission settings were largely driven by observations collected in the Walukuba site.
source: These results were largely driven by observations collected in the Walukuba site, and as such it is possible that site-specific characteristics may have driven them.
evidence: This is stated as a potential explanation for the unexpected findings in low transmission settings.

claim: Walukuba was previously a relatively high transmission rural area, but substantial decreases in transmission intensity have been observed since 2011, likely due to urbanization.
source: Walukuba was previously a relatively high transmission rural area, but substantial decreases in transmission intensity have been observed since 2011, likely due to urbanization.
evidence: This is stated as background information about the Walukuba site.

claim: Sensitivity analyses suggested that differences in the prevalence of three well characterized host-genetic polymorphisms between sites do not explain the discrepant results in low transmission settings.
source: While our sensitivity analyses suggested that differences in the prevalence of three well characterized host-genetic polymorphisms between sites do not explain these discrepant results, it is still possible that other unmeasured site-specific characteristics may have driven them.
evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analyses examining genetic factors.

claim: Lower complexity of infection coupled with lower parasite diversity in Walukuba could cause differences in immunity development, as developing an effective immune response against fewer parasite strains may be much easier than developing immunity against a more diverse pool.
source: Lower complexity of infection coupled with lower parasite diversity in Walukuba, for example, could cause this difference, as developing an effective immune response against fewer parasite strains may be much easier than developing immunity against a more diverse pool (Hviid, 1998; Bull et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about parasite diversity effects, supported by citations.

claim: It has been hypothesized that immunity may develop optimally in individuals that are exposed at a low rate, and that more frequent infections may interfere with the development of robust immune responses.
source: For example, it has been hypothesized that immunity may develop optimally in individuals that are exposed at a low rate, and that more frequent infections may interfere with the development of robust immune responses (Wipasa et al., 2010; Langhorne et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature cited to explain potential biological mechanisms.

claim: The study likely missed several asymptomatic infections, particularly in the moderate and high transmission settings, due to routine visits occurring only every 3 months.
source: With a study design including routine visits every 3 months, we are likely to have missed several asymptomatic infections, particularly in the moderate and high transmission settings.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation based on the study design.

claim: Since infections were detected using microscopy, the study was unable to detect sub-patent infections and lacked knowledge about the genetic complexity of each infection.
source: Moreover, since infections were detected using microscopy, we were unable to detect sub-patent infections, and we lack knowledge about the genetic complexity of each infection.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation based on the detection method used.

claim: Sensitivity analyses suggest that the relationships observed between age, exposure, and immunity were robust despite potential measurement error.
source: While it is possible that the expected values modeled here (expected parasite density and fever threshold) were biased by these sources of measurement error, sensitivity analyses suggest that the relationships observed were robust.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from sensitivity analyses addressing potential biases.

claim: The last decades have seen substantial declines in malaria transmission in sub-Saharan Africa that are largely attributable to increased access to effective control measures.
source: The last decades have seen substantial declines in malaria transmission in sub-Saharan Africa that are largely attributable to increased access to effective control measures, including insecticide-treated bednets, indoor residual spraying of insecticide and artemisinin-based combination therapy (Bhatt et al., 2015; World Health Organization, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In settings where transmission has been low, increased access to effective control interventions opens the possibility for malaria elimination.
source: In settings where transmission has been low, increased access to effective control interventions opens the possibility for malaria elimination.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about malaria control in low transmission settings.

claim: There are concerns that short-term decreases in malaria incidence due to reductions in transmission could be offset over time by reductions in population immunity to malaria resulting from lower exposure to parasites.
source: In highly endemic settings, however, there are concerns around the potential impact of failing to sustain interventions that reduce but do not stop transmission. Short-term decreases in malaria incidence due to reductions in transmission could be offset over time by reductions in population immunity to malaria resulting from lower exposure to parasites (Filipe et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2001; Snow et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a concern from prior literature, supported by citations.

claim: Gradual acquisition of immunity against symptomatic malaria is a key driver of the epidemiology of malaria in endemic settings.
source: Gradual acquisition of immunity against symptomatic malaria (also referred to as clinical immunity) is a key driver of the epidemiology of malaria in endemic settings, where the incidence of disease typically peaks in early childhood and then declines, while the prevalence of detectable asymptomatic parasitemia increases throughout childhood before declining in adulthood (Griffin et al., 2015; Reyburn et al., 2005; Okiro et al., 2009; Carneiro et al., 2010; Idro et al., 2006; Roca-Feltrer et al., 2010; Rodriguez-Barraquer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In endemic settings, the incidence of malaria disease typically peaks in early childhood and then declines.
source: Gradual acquisition of immunity against symptomatic malaria (also referred to as clinical immunity) is a key driver of the epidemiology of malaria in endemic settings, where the incidence of disease typically peaks in early childhood and then declines, while the prevalence of detectable asymptomatic parasitemia increases throughout childhood before declining in adulthood (Griffin et al., 2015; Reyburn et al., 2005; Okiro et al., 2009; Carneiro et al., 2010; Idro et al., 2006; Roca-Feltrer et al., 2010; Rodriguez-Barraquer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established epidemiological pattern supported by citations.

claim: In endemic settings, the prevalence of detectable asymptomatic parasitemia increases throughout childhood before declining in adulthood.
source: Gradual acquisition of immunity against symptomatic malaria (also referred to as clinical immunity) is a key driver of the epidemiology of malaria in endemic settings, where the incidence of disease typically peaks in early childhood and then declines, while the prevalence of detectable asymptomatic parasitemia increases throughout childhood before declining in adulthood (Griffin et al., 2015; Reyburn et al., 2005; Okiro et al., 2009; Carneiro et al., 2010; Idro et al., 2006; Roca-Feltrer et al., 2010; Rodriguez-Barraquer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established epidemiological pattern supported by citations.

claim: There are currently no agreed upon reliable and quantifiable immune correlates of protection that can be measured in epidemiological studies of malaria.
source: One reason it has been challenging to study immunity to malaria is that there are currently no agreed upon reliable and quantifiable immune correlates of protection that can be measured in epidemiological studies (Valletta and Recker, 2017; Fowkes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Anti-parasite immunity and anti-disease immunity have been described as independent components of clinical immunity.
source: We focus on two specific types of immunity: anti-parasite immunity (i.e. the ability to control parasite densities upon infection) and anti-disease immunity (i.e. the ability to tolerate higher parasite infections without developing objective fever), as they have been described as independent components of clinical immunity (Struik and Riley, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The study protocol was reviewed and approved by multiple ethics committees including Makerere University, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, Durham University, University of California San Francisco, and Uganda National Council for Science and Technology.
source: The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Makerere University School of Medicine Research and Ethics Committee (Identification numbers 2011–149 and 2011–167, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine Ethics Committee (Identification numbers 5943 and 5944), the Durham University School of Biological and Biomedical Sciences Ethics Committee (PRISM Entomology Uganda), the University of California, San Francisco, Committee on Human Research (Identification numbers 11–05539 and 11–05995) and the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (Identification numbers HS-978 and HS-1019).
evidence: This is stated as a factual description of the ethics approval process.

claim: All parents/guardians were asked to provide written informed consent at the time of enrollment.
source: All parents/guardians were asked to provide written informed consent at the time of enrollment.
evidence: This is stated as a factual description of the consent process.

claim: Walukuba is a peri-urban area near Lake Victoria that has the lowest transmission among the three study sites with an annual entomological inoculation rate estimated to be 2.8.
source: Walukuba, in Jinja district, is a peri-urban area near Lake Victoria that has the lowest transmission among the three (annual entomological inoculation rate (aEIR) estimated to be 2.8 [Kamya et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study site, supported by a citation.

claim: Kihihi is a rural area in southwestern Uganda characterized by moderate transmission with an aEIR of 32.
source: Kihihi, in Kanungu district, is a rural area in southwestern Uganda characterized by moderate transmission (aEIR = 32).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study site.

claim: Nagongera is a rural area in southeastern Uganda with the highest transmission with an aEIR of 310.
source: Nagongera, Tororo district, is a rural area in southeastern Uganda with the highest transmission (aEIR = 310) (Kamya et al., 2015; Kilama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study site, supported by citations.

claim: All children who reported fever in the previous 24 hr or were febrile at the time of the visit (tympanic temperature >38.0°C) were tested for malaria infection with a thick blood smear.
source: All children who reported fever in the previous 24 hr or were febrile at the time of the visit (tympanic temperature >38.0°C) were tested for malaria infection with a thick blood smear.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study protocol.

claim: If the blood smear was positive, the patient was diagnosed with symptomatic malaria and received treatment with artemether-lumefantrine (AL), the recommended first-line treatment in Uganda.
source: If the smear was positive, the patient was diagnosed with symptomatic malaria and received treatment with artemether-lumefantrine (AL), the recommended first-line treatment in Uganda.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study protocol and treatment guidelines.

claim: Episodes of complicated or recurrent malaria occurring within 14 days of therapy were treated with quinine.
source: Episodes of complicated or recurrent malaria occurring within 14 days of therapy were treated with quinine.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study protocol.

claim: Routine evaluations were performed every 3 months, including testing for asymptomatic parasitemia using thick blood smears.
source: In addition, routine evaluations were performed every 3 months, including testing for asymptomatic parasitemia using thick blood smears.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study protocol.

claim: Entomological surveys were conducted every month at all study households using miniature CDC light traps.
source: Entomological surveys were also conducted every month at all study households. During these surveys, mosquitoes were collected using miniature CDC light traps (Model 512; John W. Hock Company).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study protocol.

claim: Individual mosquitoes were tested for sporozoites using an ELISA technique.
source: Individual mosquitoes were tested for sporozoites using an ELISA technique (Kilama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the laboratory methods, supported by a citation.

claim: In Nagongera, testing for sporozoites was limited to 50 randomly selected female Anopheles mosquitoes per household per night due to the large numbers collected.
source: All female Anopheles mosquitoes captured in Walukuba and Kihihi were tested; in Nagongera testing was limited to 50 randomly selected female Anopheles mosquitoes per household per night due to the large numbers collected.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the sampling protocol.

claim: Generalized additive models (GAMs) were used to model the association between outcomes and covariates of interest.
source: In order to model the association between the outcomes and covariates of interest we used generalized additive models (gams). Gams provide a good framework, as they allow for smooth non-linear relationships.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: All models included random effects at the individual and household levels to account for lack of independence.
source: To account for lack of independence, all models included random effects at the individual (ui) and household (γi) levels.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the statistical modeling approach.

claim: Best fitting models were selected based on Akaike's Information Criterion.
source: All models were fitted in the R statistical framework using package mgcv (R Core Team, 2016). Best fitting models were selected based on Akaike's Informaiton Criterion, but changes in the percent deviance explained are also presented.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model selection approach.
